topic.name: Using Green's Theorem to Calculate Area

question.text: Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t) = 2 \sin 2t \: \mathbf{i} - 2 \sin t \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,\pi].$
question.explanation:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and

\[ \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1-0 = 1. \]

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{Area}(D) &= \iint\limits_D \textrm d A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A \\[5pt] &= -\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y \end{align*}

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = 0$ and $Q(x,y) = x,$ we get

\[ - \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = -\oint\limits_C x \: \text{d}y. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) & = 4 \cos 2t \: \mathbf{i} - 2 \cos t \: \mathbf{j}. \end{align}

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,$ as follows: \begin{align} -\oint\limits_{C} x\,\mathrm{d}y & =- \int_0^\pi 2 \sin 2t \cdot (-2 \cos t) \: \textrm{d}t \\ & = 4 \int_0^\pi \sin 2t \cos t\,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = 4 \int_0^\pi 2\sin t\cos t \cdot \cos t\,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = 8 \int_0^\pi \sin t\cos^2 t\,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = -8 \int_1^{-1} u^2 \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] & = 8 \int_{-1}^{1} u^2 \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{8}{3} u^3\Big|_{-1}^1\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{8}{3}(1^3 - (-1)^3)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16}{3} \end{align}

example.title: Calculating an Area Using Green's Theorem

question.text:
Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 3\cos t, \: 3\sin t \rangle$ for $t\in[0, 2\pi].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

\[ \text{Area}(D) = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \mathrm{d}A = \int_0^{2\pi} \fbox{$\phantom{AAAAAAA}$}\: \mathrm{d}t, \]

where $P(x,y) = 0$ and $Q(x,y) = x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
question.explanation:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and

\[ \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1 - 0 = 1. \]

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{Area}(D) &= \iint\limits_D \textrm d A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A\\[5pt] &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y \end{align*}

Substituting $P(x,y) = 0$ and $Q(x,y) = x,$ we get

\[ \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C x \: \text{d}y. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is \[ \mathbf{r}'(t) = \left\langle -3\sin t,\: 3\cos t \right\rangle. \]

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_{C} x\,\mathrm{d}y & = \int_0^{2\pi} 3\cos t \cdot 3\cos t \: \mathrm{d}t \\ & = \int_0^{2\pi} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{9\cos^2 t} \: \mathrm{d}t. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

question.text:
Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle e^{\sin t}, \: e^{\cos t} \rangle$ for $t \in \left [0, 2\pi \right].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

\[ \text{Area}(D) = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \mathrm{d}A = \int_0^{2\pi} \fbox{$\phantom{AAAAAAA}$}\: \mathrm{d}t, \]

where $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.
question.explanation:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and

\[ \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1. \]

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{Area}(D) &= \iint\limits_D \textrm d A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A\\[5pt] &= -\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y \end{align*}

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

\[ - \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is \[ \mathbf{r}'(t) = \left\langle \cos t \, e^{\sin t} ,\: -\sin t \, e^{\cos t}\right\rangle. \]

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x & = \int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos t} \cdot \cos t \, e^{\sin t}\: \mathrm{d}t \\ & = \int_0^{2\pi} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\cos t \, e^{\cos t + \sin t}} \: \mathrm{d}t. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

question.text:
Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \sin t - \sin 2t, \: \cos t - \cos 2t \rangle$ for $t \in \left[\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \right].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

\[ \text{Area}(D) = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \mathrm{d}A = \int_{\pi/3}^{5\pi/3} \fbox{$\phantom{AAAAAAA}$}\: \mathrm{d}t, \]

where $P(x,y) = 0$ and $Q(x,y) = x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.
question.explanation:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and

\[ \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1 - 0 = 1. \]

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{Area}(D) &= \iint\limits_D \textrm d A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \textrm d A \\[5pt] &= -\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y \end{align*}

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = 0$ and $Q(x,y) = x,$ we get

\[ - \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C -x \: \text{d}y. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is \[ \mathbf{r}'(t) = \left\langle \cos t - 2\cos 2t,\: -\sin t + 2\sin 2t \right\rangle. \]

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C -x \: \text{d}y & = \int_{\pi/3}^{5\pi/3} (-\sin t + \sin 2t) \cdot ( -\sin t + 2\sin 2t) \: \mathrm{d}t \\ & = \int_{\pi/3}^{5\pi/3} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(\sin 2t - \sin t)(2\sin 2t - \sin t)} \: \mathrm{d}t. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem

question.text:
Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C=C_1 \cup C_2,$ where

  • $C_1$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_1(t) = t^4 \: \mathbf{i} + t^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right],$ and

  • $C_2$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_2(t) = \: \mathbf{i} -t \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
question.explanation:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and

\[ \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1. \]

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \text{Area}(D) &= \iint\limits_D \textrm d A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A\\[5pt] &= -\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y \end{align*}

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

\[ -\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x. \]

The derivatives of $\mathbf r_1(t)$ and $\mathbf r_2(t)$ are as follows:

\begin{align} C_1: \quad & \mathbf{r}'_1(t) = 4t^3 \: \mathbf{i} +3t^2 \: \mathbf{j} \\[7pt] C_2: \quad & \mathbf{r}'_2(t) = -\mathbf{j} \\ \end{align}

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

\begin{align} \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x & =\oint\limits_{C_1 \cup C_2} y \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \oint\limits_{C_1} y \: \mathrm{d}x + \oint\limits_{C_2} y \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{-1}^{1} t^3 \cdot 4t^3 \: \textrm{d}t + \int_{-1}^{1} (-t) \cdot 0 \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = 4 \int_{-1}^{1} t^6\: \textrm{d}t - 0 \\[5pt] & = 4 \bigg[ \dfrac {t^7}{7} \bigg]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] & = 4 \cdot \dfrac{2}{7} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{8}{7}. \end{align}
